h1:
Ubon Candle Festival Trip Plan
3 Days 2 Nights
intro: The Ubon Candle Festival isn't just one parade on one day — it runs the better part of a week, and it has a rhythm to it. The carved candle floats arrive and go on display, the Home Candle night lights up the carvings after dark, and then comes the big morning parade. Time it well and you can catch every stage without elbowing your way through a hundred thousand people. This is a 3-day 2-night plan you can actually walk end to end around Thung Si Muang, with honest notes on when the sun gets brutal and which spots open early so you can eat before you stake out a viewing spot.
chips: 🆓 Free to walk around Thung Si Muang

blocks.html: Before you plan, it helps to know this is a multi-day event and each day has a different feel. In 2026 the province runs the festival from 27 July to 2 August, with the Home Candle / gathering night on 28 July — the night all the candle floats come together and the carvings are lit up. The grand candle parade runs 29–30 July, both daytime and evening, followed by the floating candle days on 31 July–1 August, which shift down to the Mun River. The exact dates move every year with the start of Buddhist Lent, but it always lands in mid-to-late July. This plan is built around the Home Candle night and the parade, the highlights most people come to see.

blocks.title: Check the dates before you book anything
blocks.html: The grand parade and the Home Candle night fall on different days, and both shift every year with the lunar calendar. Before you buy flights or book a room, confirm the dates from the Ubon City Municipality page or TAT Ubon. Rooms around Thung Si Muang fill up fast during the festival, so book several weeks ahead.

This plan is built for someone flying or driving into Ubon by the afternoon of day one, so you catch all three stages of the festival: the Home Candle night when the carvings are lit, the morning of the grand parade, and a relaxed last day walking the candle floats up close before you head home. In between, it slots in temples and a museum that sit right around Thung Si Muang — everything is within walking distance.

items: Day 1 (28 Jul — Home Candle night) — arrive in Ubon, check in near Thung Si Muang, stroll the candle floats in the evening, then watch the lit carvings on Home Candle night.
Day 2 (29 Jul — parade day) — up early to claim a viewing spot, watch the daytime candle parade, rest out of the midday sun, then come back for the evening parade.
Day 3 (30 Jul) — wander the candle floats on display up close, take it slow, drop by Wat Thung Si Muang and the museum, and grab souvenirs before heading home.

blocks.text: Day 1 — Home Candle Night, Carvings Lit Up

blocks.html: Day one is about getting in for the Home Candle night — the night every candle float gathers around Thung Si Muang and the lights come on, so the carved details stand out in a completely different way than in daylight. The crowds aren't as heavy as on parade day yet, so it's easier to wander and take photos.

blocks.label: Day 1
blocks.title: Arrive in Ubon + Home Candle Night

items.activity: Arrive in Ubon, check in near Thung Si Muang
items.note: It's under 10 minutes from Ubon airport into town. Staying near Thung Si Muang means you can walk to the festival and skip the hassle of finding parking when the roads close.

items.activity: Walk around Thung Si Muang, see the candle floats arriving
items.note: By late afternoon the sun has eased off. Take in the pre-festival atmosphere and photograph the candle floats before the crowds build.

items.activity: Isan dinner around the festival grounds
items.note: Som tam, grilled chicken, larb, and koi are easy to find around Thung Si Muang throughout the festival. Prices stay friendly, roughly THB 60–120 a dish.

items.activity: Home Candle night — candle floats lit up
items.note: The highlight of day one. The carvings really pop once the lights come on, with light shows and dance processions to watch — and no sun to fight.

items.activity: Walk and grab desserts and snacks before heading back
items.note: Isan sweets, ice cream, and street snacks run all night around the grounds. Easy to wander back to your room afterward.

blocks.title: Honest take on the Home Candle night
blocks.html: The Home Candle night is when the candle carvings look sharpest and the crowds are still thinner than on parade day. If your priority is clean photos of the floats with no one blocking the shot, this night beats the daytime parade by a long way. Don't skip it.

This is the big day. The candle parade moves around Thung Si Muang both daytime and evening, and it's the busiest day of the year. The trick is to eat breakfast early and claim a viewing spot ahead of time, because the popular spots fill up fast.

items.activity: Vietnamese kuay jab for breakfast before claiming a spot
items.note: Ubon Ocha across from Wat Maniwanaram, or Kuay Jab Dab Phloeng ("Fire Station" kuay jab), are famous breakfast spots in town — THB 50–70 a bowl and open very early. Eat before the roads close.

items.activity: Claim a viewing spot around Thung Si Muang
items.note: In front of Wat Si Ubon Rattanaram, or Lan Khwan Mueang in front of the old city hall, are where the floats stop to perform. Get there at least half an hour early — spots fill up fast.
Watch candle floats carved several meters tall roll past slowly, with dance troupes and traditional music, pausing to perform along the way.

items.activity: Escape the midday sun, find lunch in town
items.note: The sun is harshest from about 11:00–14:00, so find a shaded spot and settle in for a while. Try pho, nem nuong, or the Vietnamese noodles Ubon is known for.

items.activity: Rest in your room through the hottest part of the afternoon, save energy for the evening
items.note: The upside of staying near the grounds is that you can walk back for an afternoon nap instead of baking in the sun.

items.activity: Head back for the evening candle parade
items.note: The evening parade adds illuminated lights and light shows — a different mood from daytime, and far more comfortable in the cooler air.

items.activity: Dinner around the grounds, browse the food stalls
items.note: Isan food and street snacks around Thung Si Muang run all evening — a relaxed way to close out the big day.

blocks.title: Beat the heat and the crowds
blocks.html: The daytime parade starts around 08:30 and the sun gets strong by mid-morning. If you plan to watch for a while, bring an umbrella, a hat, and water. If you can't take the heat, or you're with kids or older travelers, watch the evening parade instead — you see the same candle floats but in far more comfort.

blocks.text: Day 3 — Candle Floats Up Close + Temples Around the Field

blocks.html: Take the last day slow. After the parade, many candle floats stay parked on display around Thung Si Muang for a close look, and the crowds have thinned right out — you can circle each float and photograph the carvings. Then it's an easy stroll to the temples and museum right next to Thung Si Muang before you pick up souvenirs and go.

blocks.label: Day 3
blocks.title: Candle Floats on Display + Temples Around Town

items.activity: Easy breakfast, then walk the candle floats on display
items.note: Many floats are still parked for you to circle and photograph up close, with far fewer people than on parade day — you can really see the carved detail.

items.activity: Stop by Wat Si Ubon Rattanaram and Wat Thung Si Muang
items.note: Important temples right by Thung Si Muang, with lovely architecture. You can walk over from the festival zone — no need to drive.

items.activity: Visit the Ubon Ratchathani National Museum
items.note: Right by Thung Si Muang. Covers the town's history and the roots of the candle festival. Entry is in the low hundreds of baht, open Wednesday–Sunday — check the day before you go.

items.activity: Farewell lunch — try Ubon's Vietnamese food
items.note: Ubon does good Vietnamese — pho and nem nuong to round things off before you pack up.

items.activity: Pick up souvenirs — moo yor and Chinese sausage — before heading home
items.note: Ubon's moo yor (Vietnamese-style pork sausage) is the famous local souvenir, with well-known shops around town. Buy the chilled kind to take home.

blocks.text: Where to Watch the Parade Around Thung Si Muang

blocks.html: The parade moves along Uparat Road onto Chayangkun Road around Thung Si Muang, with main stages where the floats stop to perform. Pick a convenient spot, settle in, and wait — you don't have to follow the parade on foot.

items.name: In front of Wat Si Ubon Rattanaram
items.blurb: A main stage by Thung Si Muang with a beautiful temple as a backdrop — great for shooting candle floats against the temple architecture. The most popular spot, so claim a place early.

items.name: Lan Khwan Mueang (in front of the old city hall)
items.blurb: A wide plaza with plenty of standing room. The floats often stop to perform here, and you can see them in full — good for groups.

items.name: Along Chayangkun Road
items.blurb: Part of the parade route, with several viewing spots. Pick a shaded one and the wait is far more comfortable when the sun is strong — and it's less crowded than in front of Wat Si Ubon.

items.name: Center of Thung Si Muang (display zone)
items.blurb: Where the floats park on display, with evening activities. Walk among them up close, with Isan food and stalls throughout the festival — best in the early evening.

blocks.text: Getting There and Where to Stay During the Festival

items: By air — several airlines fly direct from Bangkok daily, about an hour-plus in the air. It's under 10 minutes from Ubon airport into town — the easiest option if you're only coming for the festival.
By train / bus — the northeastern rail line and buses from Mo Chit run to Ubon daily, good if you're on a budget or want to sleep on the way. Book tickets ahead during the festival.
Staying near Thung Si Muang — fills up fast during the festival, so book several weeks ahead. Staying near the grounds is well worth it since you can walk back to rest in the afternoon.

Getting around during the festival — on parade day, several roads around Thung Si Muang close. If you drive, park a bit further out and walk in. Staying near the grounds cuts this problem out entirely.

blocks.title: If you have fewer than 3 days
blocks.html: With only 2 days and 1 night, drop the first day — arrive in time for the Home Candle night in the evening and watch the parade the next morning, and you've still hit the highlights. If you genuinely have just one day, come on the grand parade day and catch the morning parade then the evening one all in a single day.

faq.q: When is the Ubon Candle Festival in 2026?
faq.a: In 2026 the province runs the festival from 27 July to 2 August, with the gathering / Home Candle night on 28 July, the grand candle parade (both daytime and evening) on 29–30 July, and the floating candle days along the Mun River on 31 July–1 August. The dates shift every year with the start of Buddhist Lent, so check the Ubon City Municipality page before you travel.

faq.q: How many days do you need for the Ubon Candle Festival?
faq.a: Three days and two nights covers every stage of the festival: day one catches the Home Candle night with the carvings lit up, day two is the grand parade both daytime and evening, and day three is for walking the candle floats on display up close, plus the temples and museum around Thung Si Muang. If you have less time, 2 days and 1 night still covers the highlights.

faq.q: Where's the best spot to watch the candle parade?
faq.a: The main stages are around Thung Si Muang — for example, in front of Wat Si Ubon Rattanaram, which has the temple as a backdrop, and Lan Khwan Mueang in front of the old city hall, where the floats stop to perform. Both fill up fast, so get there at least half an hour early. If you want to see the carvings up close, go when the floats are parked on display in the center of Thung Si Muang.

faq.q: How is the Home Candle night different from the parade day?
faq.a: The Home Candle night is when all the candle floats gather around Thung Si Muang and the carvings are lit up — the detail stands out sharply and the crowds are still thinner than on parade day, so it's great for close-up photos. The parade day is when the floats move in procession with dance troupes and music — the busiest day of the year, and you can watch both daytime and evening.

faq.q: Is there an entry fee for the Ubon Candle Festival, and should you book a room ahead?
faq.a: The festival is free to walk all day — it's a public event around Thung Si Muang, with costs only for food and lodging. Rooms during the festival fill up fast, especially hotels around Thung Si Muang, so book several weeks ahead to be within walking distance of the grounds and able to come back to rest in the afternoon.
